rv.q: I left this lovely, subtle, intelligent show in a melancholy daze.
Rourke’s production is beautifully pitched: even as the women tease and bicker, and coax music out of their erratic new wireless, there’s a shadow of sadness to it.
Josie Rourke’s sumptuous and thoughtful staging of Dancing at Lughnasa shows why this 1990 play is so loved.

Movement lies at the emotional heart of this play and it is orchestrated with such delicate mastery by Wayne McGregor that the stomping scene, featuring the sisters dancing with wild abandon is a shared hedonistic escape, rebellious ritual and act of worship in one.
Even if you missed all the subtext, this show would still delight in its acute depiction of family dynamics...This play won Friel the Award for best play in 1991, and it still looks richly deserved.
In a glorious performance of quiet luminosity, Mitchell gradually unpeels layers of the seemingly strait-laced Kate's complexity.
It is a production of piercing lyricism as well as embracing warmth and wit: gorgeous.
The crux of ‘Dancing at Lughnasa’ is that it’s a sort of happy tragedy...It’s not bliss, but it is community, safety, sisterhood warmth, and dancing. A beautiful production of a beautiful play.

The performances – from Justice Mitchell’s hardbitten, scolding eldest Kate, to Ardal O’Hanlon’s endearingly confused Jack – can’t be faulted but, like that temperamental Marconi, their full force is felt a tad too intermittently.
The evening is bathed in charm and quiet desolation but it seldom rises above the merely watchable.
Yet I still find the piece, even when it’s performed with conviction, as it is here, naggingly schematic and sometimes shamelessly sentimental.
I was left pining for the gut-churning conflict of loss and longing that can make Friel's writing a great deal more potent.
It is a glory, full of emotion and power.
As enchanting as this setting is, it's also ruled by pitiless patriarchal Catholicism.
These are all fine performances individually and as an excellent ensemble, a real family.
Dancing at Lughnasa definitely deserves the moniker.
This production may throw different aspects of the play into bold relief...but the play's sense of ectasy dampened down by circumstance.
There are excellent performances from the five sisters in this engaging and deeply reflective show.
Ultimately one wonders what director, Josie Rourke, intended to make of the work in its second production at Theatre, having also played at The Old Vic in 2009 and around the world.
Famine zones are more fun than this play and yet Brian Friel's shrieking bumpkins are exactly what the Arts Council wants us to see.

cn.t: Friel's memory play receives a sumptuous, beautifully detailed revival that captures its elegiac poetry and warmth, though some critics find the pacing slow and emotional impact softened by the Olivier's scale.
